lessons.title: What Is Geography?
lessons.notes_html:
Meaning of the Word Geography

The word "Geography" is a combination of two words, Geo and Graphy. Geo means Earth and Graphy means description, so Geography means "Description of the Earth".

What Geography Studies

Geography is the study of the overall surroundings of the physical and human environment. Modern geography studies the Earth as the home of man. It tries to find out the relationship between man and his environment — in other words, it studies man's adaptation to the environment in which he lives and works.

  • "Geography is the science of places."
  • "Geography is a scientific or systematic study of areal variations and similarities from place to place on the surface of the Earth."

What We See Around Us

The Earth's surface shows many physical features, such as rivers, mountains, plains, deserts and the atmosphere above it. Geography describes all these features and how people live among them.

lessons.title: Internal Structure of the Earth
lessons.notes_html:
How Do We Know What Is Inside the Earth?

Information about the internal structure of the Earth is limited. The distance between the Earth's surface and its centre is 6371 km. Scientists take help from earthquake waves, the magnetic force of the Earth and gravitational force to get information about the internal structure of the Earth.

The information from these sources revealed that the internal structure of the Earth is composed of three layers: the crust, the mantle and the core.

The Three Layers at a Glance

LayerPositionMain feature
CrustOutermost layerThin layer on which oceans and continents exist
MantleCentral (middle) layerAbout 2900 km deep
CoreInnermost layerMade of iron and nickel (Nife)

Comparing the Earth with an Egg

The Earth can be compared with an egg, because both have a thin outer shell, a middle layer and a central part. The eggshell is like the thin crust, the egg white is like the mantle, and the yolk is like the core at the centre. The comparison helps us remember that the crust is very thin compared with the whole Earth, just as the shell is thin compared with the whole egg.

mcqs.why: The distance between the Earth's surface and its centre is 6371 km, which is why direct information about the inside is limited.

mcqs.why: Scientists use earthquake waves, the magnetic force of the Earth and gravitational force to get information about the internal structure of the Earth.

lessons.title: The Earth's Crust: Continental and Oceanic
lessons.notes_html:
Earth's Crust

The outermost part of the Earth, at which oceans and continents exist, is known as the Earth's crust. Its depth varies from about 16 km to 40 km due to the uneven distribution of physical features on the Earth. It is further divided into two main parts: continental crust and oceanic crust.

Continental Crust

The continental crust consists of various land masses known as continents. It is comprised of silicon and aluminium, so it is also known as Sial. Its maximum depth is about 40 km.

Oceanic Crust

The part of the Earth's crust under oceanic water, in the form of the ocean bed, is called the oceanic crust. Its depth is about 8 km. It contains silicon and magnesium and is named as Sima.

Continental crust (Sial)Oceanic crust (Sima)
Made ofSilicon and aluminiumSilicon and magnesium
DepthAbout 40 kmAbout 8 km
FoundUnder the continentsUnder the oceans (ocean bed)

lessons.title: Mantle and Core
lessons.notes_html:
Mantle

The central layer of the Earth, after the crust, is the mantle. Its depth is around 2900 km.

  • The upper part of the mantle is in molten form, and its temperature is about 2000°C.
  • The lower mantle is solid, and its temperature is about 3000°C. Although the temperature of the lower mantle is higher than the upper mantle, it is in solid form due to the higher pressure of the upper mantle and crust.

Core

The core is the innermost layer of the Earth. It is divided into two parts, the outer core and the inner core.

  • Outer core — in liquid form; its depth is about 2250 km and its temperature is about 3800°C.
  • Inner core — in solid form; its depth is about 1220 km deep, and its average temperature is about 5200°C.

The core contains the rocks of iron and nickel and is also known as Nife.

How Hot Is the Inside of the Earth?

The average temperature of the inner core is about 5000°C. The temperature increases as we go from the surface towards the centre of the Earth.

lessons.title: Tectonic Plates
lessons.notes_html:
Pangaea — the Super Continent

All the continents were once like a giant super continent. Millions of years ago it was named as "Pangaea" by a scientist named Wegener. Pangaea was divided into smaller pieces (plates) and adopted the form of the present continents due to the internal movements of the Earth.

The Major Tectonic Plates

The crust is divided into the following seven major plates and many other minor plates:

  • Pacific Plate
  • North American Plate
  • South American Plate
  • African Plate
  • Eurasian Plate
  • Indo-Australian Plate
  • Antarctic Plate

Plates Are Always Moving

The Earth's crust is solid and floats on the upper part of the mantle, which is called molten. Hence these plates are not static but always remain in motion. The Ring of Fire, where many volcanoes and earthquakes occur, is located in the Pacific Ocean.

lessons.title: Types of Rocks
lessons.notes_html:
Three Types of Rocks

Rocks are of three main types: igneous rocks, sedimentary rocks and metamorphic rocks. Each type is formed in a different way.

Igneous Rocks: Intrusive and Extrusive

  • Intrusive igneous rocks are formed by the solidification of magma in cracks beneath the Earth's surface. Examples are gabbro, diorite and dolerite.
  • Extrusive igneous rocks are formed by the solidification of lava at the Earth's surface, where it cools immediately. Examples are basalt and obsidian.

Sedimentary Rocks

Sedimentary rocks are formed on the surface of the Earth from weathered and eroded material (sediments) deposited layer by layer. The sediments are transported to far-off places, deposited in layers, and fixed together firmly with the passage of time. Examples are limestone, shale, sandstone, conglomerate and breccia.

Metamorphic Rocks

Rocks that have changed their properties due to pressure and temperature (heat and pressure) are called metamorphic rocks. Marble is an example of a metamorphic rock.

Type of rockHow it is formedExamples
IgneousCooling and solidification of magma or lavaGabbro, diorite, dolerite, basalt, obsidian
SedimentarySediments deposited layer by layer and fixed togetherLimestone, shale, sandstone, conglomerate, breccia
MetamorphicEarlier rocks changed by heat and pressureMarble, slate

lessons.title: The Rock Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
What Is the Rock Cycle?

The rock cycle is the process of making and breaking of rocks. It shows how one type of rock changes into another, again and again.

How the Rock Cycle Works

  • Weathering and erosion break rocks into small pieces.
  • Agents like rivers, winds and glaciers transport this material and redeposit it.
  • The deposited material becomes sedimentary rock.
  • Heat and pressure change it into metamorphic rock.
  • Melting and cooling turn it back into igneous rock — and so the cycle continues.

lessons.title: Rocks and Minerals in Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Rocks Commonly Found in Pakistan

All three main types of rocks are located in Pakistan.

  • Igneous rocks — obsidian at Chaghi (Balochistan), basalt at Ranikot (Sindh) and gabbro at Zhob (Balochistan).
  • Sedimentary rocks — limestone is mostly found in the northern and western mountainous areas of Pakistan.
  • Metamorphic rocks — marble is found in the country, and rocks such as marble and slate are formed where earlier rocks changed under heat and pressure. The northern mountain areas of Pakistan, where the Eurasian and Indo-Australian plates collide, are rich in such rocks.

Why Are Rocks Important for Us?

Rocks are important because they provide building material, cement, salt, chalk and many minerals used in daily life and industry. They also form the soil in which crops grow, and the study of rocks tells us about the history of the Earth. Without rocks there would be no mountains, no soil and no mineral wealth.

Importance of Minerals for the Economy

Minerals are important for the economy of any country because they are used in industry, construction, medicines, bleaches and soaps, and food preservation. Rocks like gypsum and limestone are used in the cement industry, and rock salt is part of our daily food. A country rich in minerals can develop its industry and trade, and mining itself provides work for many people.

lessons.title: Modern Techniques in Geography: GIS, RS, GPS and Google Maps
lessons.notes_html:
Modern Techniques in the Field of Geography

Modern techniques in geography are the Geographical Information System (GIS), Remote Sensing (RS), the Global Positioning System (GPS) and Google Maps.

Remote Sensing and GIS

In remote sensing, satellites collect useful information in the form of images, which are then processed using GIS. This makes it easier to study inaccessible areas.

Global Positioning System (GPS)

GPS helps people in positioning and travelling. Signals from different satellites are received on the Earth by control stations, and the user receives that information through a device. It is extremely helpful for tracking companies, travellers, army navigators and tourists.

Google Maps

Google Maps, easily accessible through smart phones, gives information about sites, road networks, traffic conditions and geographical regions.

Impacts of Modern Technology in Geography

Modern technology has made the study of geography faster, more accurate and possible even for inaccessible areas. Satellite images, GIS maps and GPS positioning help in planning, travelling, tracking and emergency services. At the same time, people must learn to use these tools correctly, because a map or a satellite image is only useful when it is read and interpreted properly.

lessons.title: What Is a Mountain?
lessons.notes_html:
Definition of a Mountain

A landmass on the Earth's surface with a rocky, uneven, sloppy and elevated surface is known as a mountain. Mountains rise much higher than the land around them and usually have steep slopes.

  • The highest mountain peak in the world is Mount Everest (8848 m), in the Himalayas.
  • The Rockies are located in North America.

lessons.title: Types of Mountains
lessons.notes_html:
Three Types of Mountains

There are three broad types of mountains according to their formation: folded mountains, block mountains and volcanic mountains.

Folded Mountains

Folded mountains are formed by the convergence of tectonic plates, which produces folds. The Himalayas, Rockies, Andes and Alps are examples, and the Himalayas hold the world's highest peak, Mount Everest (8848 m).

Block Mountains

Block mountains are formed when the Earth's crust cracks due to divergence and a block between faults is uplifted. The uplifted block is called a horst, and the sunken part between faults forms a rift valley or graben; the Harz Mountains of Germany are an example.

Volcanic Mountains

Volcanic mountains are formed when lava accumulates and solidifies layer by layer into a conical shape. Vesuvius in Italy and Fujiyama in Japan are famous examples. There are three types of volcanic mountains: cinder cone, composite and shield volcanoes.

TypeHow formedExamples
Folded mountainsConvergence of tectonic plates produces foldsHimalayas, Rockies, Andes, Alps
Block mountainsCrust cracks; a block between faults is upliftedHarz Mountains (Germany)
Volcanic mountainsLava accumulates and solidifies layer by layerVesuvius (Italy), Fujiyama (Japan)

Fold and Fault

A fold is a bend in the layers of rock produced when tectonic plates converge and press the crust together; the upper part of a fold is called an anticline and the lower part a syncline. A fault is a crack in the Earth's crust produced by the movement of plates, along which blocks of crust move up, down or sideways.

What Is a Rift Valley?

A rift valley is a feature associated with block mountains. It is formed when the Earth's crust on both sides of two parallel faults is uplifted or sinks, leaving a low valley between them.

  • The Great Basin of the USA

lessons.title: Plateaus: Piedmont and Continental
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Plateau?

Plateaus are flat, elevated areas of land. The book describes piedmont and continental plateaus in particular.

Piedmont Plateaus

Piedmont plateaus are located at the foothills of mountains and are surrounded by mountains on one side and ocean or plain on the other. Examples are the Patagonia Plateau in South America and the Potwar Plateau in Pakistan, in the piedmonts of the Himalayas.

The Potwar Plateau

The Potwar Plateau lies south of the Siwalik hills, between the rivers Jhelum and Indus, with the Salt Range to its south, and it is rich in oil and gas exploration sites.

Continental Plateaus

A continental plateau is a large, flat, elevated area of land that rises above the surrounding plains. Unlike a piedmont plateau at the foothills of mountains, a continental plateau lies in the interior of a continent and is surrounded by plains or oceans on its sides.

lessons.notes_html:
V-Shaped Valleys

A V-shape valley is a valley cut by a river in mountainous areas. The river erodes downwards, so the valley becomes deeper and takes the shape of the English alphabet 'V'. A river forms a V-shaped valley. Very deep V-shape valleys are often called gorges, and such valleys are found in the northern areas of Pakistan.

Importance of Valleys for Pakistan

Valleys are important for Pakistan because they provide flat, fertile land for farming and settlement between mountains, and their rivers provide water for crops and daily life. Beautiful valleys like Naran attract tourists, which supports hotels and local trade. Valleys also provide routes through mountains for roads and communication between different regions.

lessons.title: Mountains of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Famous Mountain Ranges of Pakistan

Pakistan is surrounded by mighty mountain ranges from the northern and western sides. Famous mountain ranges in Pakistan are:

  • The Himalayas (Lesser and Greater Himalayas)
  • The Karakoram
  • The Hindukush
  • The Suleman Range
  • The Kirthar Range
  • The Salt Range
  • The Toba Kakar mountains (to the west and south-west)

Great Peaks of Pakistan

  • The highest peak of the Karakoram is K-2. The Karakoram range runs from Gilgit to Skardu.
  • The highest peak of the Greater Himalayas in Pakistan is Nanga Parbat (8126 metres). In the north, the Greater Himalayas include Gilgit, Swat and Kohistan.

Valleys and Glaciers

Murree, Galiyat, Kaghan and Abbottabad are significant valleys in the Himalayas, and glaciers on these mountains continue their creeping movement along the slopes.

How the Himalayas Are Important for Pakistan

The Himalayas are important for Pakistan because they store snow and feed the rivers that water the plains, and they protect the country from cold northern winds. Their valleys support tourism, and their forests and minerals support the local economy. They also cause rainfall, because the monsoon winds strike these mountains and bring rain to the country.

lessons.title: Impacts of Mountains on Human Life
lessons.notes_html:
How Mountains Affect Human Life

Mountains affect human life in many ways. They control climate, because mountain areas are colder and receive more rain and snow, and they are the source of rivers that water the plains.

Work in Mountain Areas

The people of mountain areas work in handicrafts, farming, tourism and hoteling, and beautiful valleys like Naran attract visitors.

Difficulties of Mountain Life

At the same time, life in mountains is hard because of steep land, cold winters and difficult transport, and mountain areas are also the site of natural hazards like landslides and earthquakes.

Physical Regions of Pakistan and People's Life

The physical regions of Pakistan shape how people live and work. In the northern and north-western mountainous areas the climate is cold, some areas remain snow-covered all year, and people work in handicrafts, farming, tourism and hoteling. In the plains the climate is extreme — winters cold and summers warm — the soil brought by rivers is favourable for agriculture, and most people depend directly or indirectly on farming.

Impacts of Earthquakes on the Ecosystem

An earthquake shakes and jerks the Earth's crust due to seismic waves, and it damages buildings, roads, water supply and drainage systems. It can cause landslides, change the course of rivers and destroy forests and animal habitats. After an earthquake, the ecosystem takes a long time to recover, because soil, water and vegetation are all disturbed at once.

lessons.title: Weather and Climate
lessons.notes_html:
Weather

Weather is the atmospheric condition of temperature, rainfall, air pressure and amount of humidity at a particular place at a particular time. Weather is the short-term atmospheric condition of a place.

Climate

Climate is actually the average of weather conditions over a longer period of time.

Factors Affecting the Climate of a Place

  • Latitude — equatorial areas are hotter and polar areas are colder.
  • Altitude — temperature falls with height.
  • Distance from the sea — coastal areas remain moderate.
  • Winds, mountains and rainfall — mountains like the Himalayas interact with monsoon winds and cause rainfall.

lessons.title: Climatic Regions of the World
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Climatic Region?

A climatic region is an area roughly demarcated by lines of latitude, into which the Earth can be divided on the basis of climate. Areas in the same climatic region have similar temperature, rainfall and seasons.

The Four Climatic Regions

The different climatic regions of the world are:

  • The equatorial region — hotter
  • The tropical region
  • The temperate region — moderate
  • The polar region — colder

Why Are Climatic Zones Different?

Climatic zones of the world are different because the Sun's rays do not fall equally on all parts of the Earth. Areas near the equator receive direct rays and are hot, while areas near the poles receive slanting rays and are cold. Latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, winds and mountains add further differences, so each zone has its own temperature and rainfall pattern.

lessons.notes_html:
The Tropical Region

The tropical climatic region lies between the equatorial and temperate regions. In the book's forest classification it lies roughly between 30° N and 30° S. It is hot with short, cool winters.

  • The Sahara Desert is located in the tropical climatic region.
  • The main profession of the people living in the tropical area is agriculture.
  • Land and sea breezes blow in coastal areas.

Monsoon Winds

Monsoon winds blow in the tropical region. More than three-quarters of Pakistan's rainfall comes from the summer monsoon. The monsoon winds bring rain to the plains and to the lower slopes of the Himalayas, which receive maximum rainfall in Pakistan. The northern mountains, the north-western region and the western part of the plains also get sufficient rainfall from the western disturbance in winter. In coastal areas, tropical storms from the Arabian Sea and thunderstorms associated with thermal instability produce some rainfall.

Life and Crops in the Tropical Region

The region is rich in mineral resources, so people are engaged in mining as well as agriculture, and high-quality cotton, wheat, rice and sugarcane are cultivated there.

Vegetation in the polar climatic region is very poor, because the region is extremely cold and covered with snow and ice for most of the year. Only mosses, lichens and a few small hardy plants can grow in the short summer.

lessons.title: Importance of Climate in Human Life
lessons.notes_html:
Climate and Human Activities

Climate has significant impacts on human life, because all economic, social, political and commercial activities of people in any area are based on climate. Human activities, lifestyles, customs and traditions vary from place to place with climate.

Climate and Houses

Houses are built differently in different climates: roofs are sloppy (sloping) in areas of heavy snowfall, and highly elevated and wide in hotter areas to avoid heat.

Climate, Animals and Agriculture

Climate affects animals too — for example, the camel survives in deserts without water for days. It affects agriculture at large, because temperature, humidity, rainfall and evaporation decide which crops grow where, such as wheat in the temperate region and rice and rubber in the equatorial and monsoon regions.

How Climate Affects Our Daily Life

Climate affects our life because it decides what we wear, what we eat, what kind of house we build and what work we do. Farmers depend on rainfall and temperature for their crops, and traders, travellers and builders all plan their work according to the season. In short, no part of daily life is free from the effect of climate.

Impacts of Vegetation on Our Climate

Vegetation affects climate because forests give out moisture through transpiration, cool the air and bring rainfall. When forests are cut down, the land becomes hotter and drier, rainfall decreases and soil erosion increases. That is why the book says forests must ideally cover 25% of a country's area for ideal climatic conditions.

lessons.title: Types of Forests in the World
lessons.notes_html:
Three Main Types of Forests

There are three main types of forests in the world: tropical forests, temperate forests and boreal forests.

Tropical Forests

Tropical forests are situated in equatorial and sub-equatorial areas between 30° N to 30° S. These areas are hot with short, cool winters, and the season remains almost the same throughout the year, so dense vegetation grows there. The most common type of tropical forest is the evergreen rainforest, found in the equatorial belt including parts of Africa, Southeast Asia and South and Central America, where trees are taller and highly dense, and most rainforest trees are hardwoods.

Temperate Forests

Temperate forests are situated in temperate areas, with annual precipitation ranging from 750 mm to 1750 mm. In the book's classification they lie between the tropical and boreal zones, in regions with moderate temperature and four seasons.

Forests of the World

  • Two famous forests of the world are the Amazon forests of South America and the Zaire Basin forests of Africa (the Zaire Basin is located in Africa). Both are rainforests in the equatorial belt, and the Amazon is the largest rainforest in the world.
  • Forests above the height of 4000 metres are Alpine forests.

lessons.title: Layers of Rainforests
lessons.notes_html:
Four Layers of a Rainforest

Rainforests have four layers: the emergent layer, the canopy layer, the understory and the ground layer.

Emergent Layer

The emergent layer is the uppermost layer, where the tallest trees rise above the surroundings; their average height is 40–55 metres. They are found in limited numbers, and bats, certain monkeys and butterflies live here. The tallest trees are found in the emergent layer.

Canopy Layer

The canopy layer is formed by tall trees with an average height of 30–40 metres, which are extremely close to each other so that their crowns mix up to form a continuous canopy. This layer does not let sunlight penetrate to the layers below, and non-parasitic plants like lianas and epiphytes are also found in this layer.

Understory and Ground Layer

Below the canopy is the understory layer of smaller trees and shrubs growing in shade, and at the bottom is the ground layer of herbs, ferns and fallen leaves on the forest floor.

lessons.title: Importance of Forests
lessons.notes_html:
Importance of the Amazon Rainforest

The Amazon rainforest is important because it is the largest rainforest in the world and it controls the climate of its region by giving out moisture and absorbing carbon dioxide. It is home to countless species of plants and animals, and its trees provide timber, medicines and oxygen. Its destruction would disturb rainfall, climate and wildlife far beyond South America.

Role of Forests in the Economy of a Country

Forests play a great role in the economy of a country. They provide timber for construction and furniture, fuel wood, paper pulp, medicines, fruits and honey, and they give work to people in forestry, tourism and related industries. Forests boost economic activities by providing raw material for paper and furniture industries, and by protecting soil and water they support farming, which is the main economic activity of the country.

How Forests Prevent Soil Erosion

Forests prevent soil erosion because the roots of trees hold the soil firmly together, so rain and wind cannot wash it away easily. The leaves and fallen litter also break the force of rain, and the forest floor absorbs water, so less water runs off the surface carrying soil with it.

Importance of Forests for Our Environment

Forests are important for our environment because they are an essential part of the ecosystem. They clean the air, give out oxygen, bring rainfall, protect soil from erosion and provide shelter for wildlife. Without forests, the climate would become drier, floods would increase and many species would lose their homes.

lessons.notes_html:
How Much of Pakistan Is Covered by Forests?

Only about 5% of Pakistan's area is covered by forests, while ideally forests must cover 25% of a country's area, so Pakistan needs to increase its forest cover.

Distribution of Forests in Pakistan

Forests in Pakistan are distributed according to climate and rainfall:

  • Coniferous forests grow in the northern mountain areas.
  • Riverine forests grow along the Indus and its tributaries.
  • Irrigated plantations like Changa Manga grow in the plains, where water is supplied by canals. Changa Manga is an example of an irrigated plantation.
  • Scrub forests (rakhs) grow in dry areas.
  • The Chiltan National Park near Quetta is an important protected forest area of the country.

Why Forests Are Different in Different Areas of Pakistan

Forests are different in different areas of Pakistan because natural vegetation is greatly influenced by climate, especially precipitation and temperature. Areas with more than 100 cm of rainfall support forests, areas with 25–100 cm support grasslands, and areas with less than 25 cm support only desert vegetation. That is why the north has coniferous forests, the river plains have riverine forests and the dry areas have only scrub.

Impacts of Northern Forests on Climate

The northern forests of Pakistan make the climate of those areas cooler and wetter, because trees give out moisture and shade the land. They hold snow and rainwater in the soil, feed streams and rivers, and protect the mountain slopes from erosion. When these forests are cut, the area becomes drier and landslides become more common.

lessons.title: Deforestation

What Is Deforestation?

Deforestation is the elimination of forests to get agricultural or residential land. When trees are cut down on a large scale, the land loses its cover, the climate becomes drier and soil erosion increases.

How We Can Reduce Deforestation in Pakistan

  • Plant new trees for every tree cut down.
  • Protect existing forests with strict laws and forest guards.
  • Give people alternative fuel and building material so they do not need to cut forests.
  • Create public awareness; national parks like Chiltan and irrigated plantations like Changa Manga also help to increase forest cover and protect the environment.

Agriculture and Vegetation

Agriculture is the growing and harvesting of crops in a particular natural and human environment; plants in agriculture do not grow automatically but are controlled by humans, and agriculture is an activity done by farmers to yield crops. Vegetation is the natural plant cover of an area, such as forests, grasslands, mosses, lichens, algae and shrubs, which grows without human control and is greatly influenced by climate.

lessons.title: What Are Natural Disasters?
lessons.notes_html:
Definition of Natural Disasters

Natural disasters are sudden, harmful events caused by natural forces, such as floods, tsunamis, cyclones and earthquakes. They damage life, property, crops and the environment, and they are beyond human control, although human activities can increase their frequency and damage.

Examples of Natural Disasters

Natural disasters mean the destructive events of nature that cause great loss of life and property. Examples given in the book are floods, tsunamis, cyclones and earthquakes, and also drought, landslides and volcanic eruptions, which disturb the normal life of an area.

Facts to Remember

  • The overflow of water from rivers is called a flood. The most common natural disaster in Pakistan is the flood.
  • The result of the absence of rainfall for a longer period of time is known as drought.
  • Landsliding occurs mostly in mountainous areas.
  • In 1935, an earthquake demolished the city of Quetta in Balochistan.
  • World Environment Day is observed on 5th June.

lessons.notes_html:
Floods

Floods occur when rivers overflow and bring vast areas of land under water, damaging crops, houses and roads.

Earthquakes

Earthquakes are the shaking and jerking of the Earth's crust due to seismic waves. They demolish buildings, block water supply and drainage due to infrastructural damage, and in 1935 an earthquake demolished Quetta in Balochistan.

Drought

Drought is the absence of rainfall for a long period in an area. Three impacts of drought are:

  • Crops fail because there is no rain for a long period, so farmers lose their income and food becomes scarce.
  • Water sources dry up, so people and animals suffer from shortage of drinking water.
  • The soil becomes dry and dusty, which increases dust storms and damages the environment.

Primary Impacts of Natural Disasters

The primary impacts of natural disasters are the direct damages they cause at once. Floods bring vast areas of land under water and damage crops, earthquakes shake buildings and break roads and water supply, and landslides block drainage and destroy houses and fields in mountainous areas.

How Global Warming Causes Natural Disasters

Global warming causes natural disasters because the greenhouse effect is increasing in the atmosphere day by day due to human activities, and the Earth's temperature is rising.

Why Disasters Are Becoming More Frequent

  • Higher temperature melts glaciers and raises sea level, which increases floods and tsunamis.
  • It changes rainfall patterns, causing droughts in some areas and heavy rain in others.
  • It makes storms and cyclones stronger.

That is why floods, the most common disaster in Pakistan, are occurring more frequently now.

Impacts of Rising Temperature on Our Environment

Rising temperature melts glaciers and snow, raises sea level and changes rainfall patterns, so some areas face floods and others face drought. It increases heatwaves, dust storms and forest fires, damages crops and disturbs wildlife. In Pakistan, rising temperature also increases the melting of mountain snow, which feeds floods in the plains.

Human Activities Responsible for Natural Disasters

  • Cutting down forests, which increases floods, droughts and landslides.
  • Burning fossil fuels, which increases the greenhouse effect and global warming.
  • Building on flood plains, river banks and unstable slopes, which increases damage when floods and landslides occur.
  • Pollution of air and water and careless use of land, which make the environment weaker against natural hazards.

Why Floods Are Occurring Frequently in Pakistan

Floods are occurring frequently in Pakistan because of heavy monsoon rains, melting of mountain snow due to rising temperature, and cutting down of forests, which increases run-off. Rivers overflow their banks and bring vast areas under water, and building on flood plains increases the damage.

Why Developing Countries Are the Most Affected

Developing countries are the most affected by natural disasters because they have insufficient early warning systems for natural hazards. Their buildings and infrastructure are weaker, people are poorer and live in vulnerable areas like flood plains and unstable slopes, and after a disaster they have fewer resources for rescue, relief and rebuilding.

lessons.title: Preservation of Natural Resources
lessons.notes_html:
Why Natural Resources Must Be Preserved

Natural resources must be preserved because they are limited and human life depends on them for food, water, fuel, timber and minerals.

Measures for Preservation of Natural Resources

  • Plant forests to the ideal 25% cover and protect wildlife in national parks.
  • Use water carefully and without waste.
  • Follow the three Rs (reduce, recycle, reuse).
  • Use renewable energy instead of burning fossil fuels.
  • Awareness and strict laws against overuse also help.

The Three Rs: Reduce, Recycle, Reuse

The three Rs mean reduce, recycle and reuse. Reduce means using fewer resources and producing less waste; recycle means processing used material like paper, plastic and glass into new products; and reuse means using the same thing again instead of throwing it away. Following the three Rs saves resources and protects the environment. Every person can help by reducing waste in daily life.

lessons.title: Weathering and Erosion
lessons.notes_html:
Weathering

Weathering is the disintegration of rocks into smaller particles, and the process of weathering is mostly seen in dry and cold areas.

Erosion

Erosion is the carrying away of the weathered material by agents like rivers, glaciers and wind, which continuously do their work and make different types of landforms on the Earth's surface.

Types of Weathering

There are three types of weathering:

  • Physical weathering — the breaking of rocks into smaller pieces by physical forces like heat, cold and pressure, mostly seen in dry and cold areas.
  • Chemical weathering — the weakening and breaking of rocks by chemical processes. Seawater is saline, and eroded material carried by waves reacts with mineral particles in the water and is dissolved, which weakens the coast; this process is called solution. Acid rain due to air pollution also results in chemical weathering of rocks.
  • Biological weathering — weathering due to living organisms on the Earth's surface, such as the roots of plants growing into cracks and animals burrowing into rocks.

Agents of Weathering and Erosion

The agents of weathering and erosion are rivers, glaciers and wind, and also the sea in coastal areas. Heat, rain, wind, rivers and glaciers are the main agents in the formation of sedimentary rocks.

lessons.title: Coastal Erosion and Its Landforms
lessons.notes_html:
Processes of Coastal Erosion

In coastal erosion the four processes involved are corrasion, attrition, solution and hydraulic action.

Landforms Made by Coastal Erosion

  • Caves — continuous wave attack at the bottom of cliffs creates cavities which become caves.
  • Headland and bay — sometimes sea water invades farther inland, creating a bay (a circular and small part of the sea), while the bordering land of hard rocks remains ahead in the water as a headland.
  • Sea arch — sea waves striking the headland from both sides create an opening through the headland.
  • Stack — when the sea arch is detached from the headland by further erosion, the remaining column-like structure stands alone in the sea. Such landforms can be seen in the coastal areas of Pakistan, especially at Hawksbay.
  • Sea cliffs — on mountainous coasts, seaward slopes exposed by wave attack retreat and become perpendicular sea cliffs.

Parts of a Wave

The upper part of a wave is called the crest.

lessons.title: Wind Erosion
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Wind Erosion?

Wind erosion is the erosion done by wind, which works notably in arid and semi-arid areas like Balochistan in Pakistan — the most arid province of Pakistan. Wind performs its erosional work in two ways:

  • Deflation — carrying unconsolidated (loose) sediments with it.
  • Abrasion — using these sediments as a tool for further erosion.

Landforms Made by Wind Erosion

By deflation and abrasion, wind wears down rocks and forms zeugen, mushroom rocks, deflation basins, yardangs and inselbergs. A rock eroded from the base due to aeolian (wind) work is called a mushroom rock.

Water Erosion and Wind Erosion

Water erosion is done by rivers and sea waves. A river breaks rocks in its way, transports the eroded material and deposits it when its speed becomes very low, forming V-shape valleys, waterfalls, pot holes, meanders, ox-bow lakes and deltas. Wind erosion works in arid and semi-arid areas, carrying loose sediments away by deflation and wearing down rocks by abrasion.

lessons.title: Human Activities and Erosion of Land
lessons.notes_html:
Role of Human Activities in Erosion of Land

Human activities increase erosion of land in many ways:

  • Cutting down forests removes the roots that hold soil, so rain and wind wash the soil away easily.
  • Ploughing, mining, construction and clearing land for agriculture expose the soil to wind and water.
  • Pollution causes acid rain, which results in chemical weathering.

On the other hand, planting trees, building terraces and protecting vegetation can reduce erosion and protect the land.

How Weathering and Erosion Form Soil

Weathering and erosion are important in the formation of soil because weathering first disintegrates rocks into smaller particles, and erosion then transports and deposits this material in new places. Over time, the deposited material mixes with organic matter and becomes soil, in which plants can grow. Without weathering there would be no broken rock material, and without erosion there would be no transport of that material to form soil elsewhere.

How We May Stop Deforestation

We may stop deforestation by planting new trees for every tree cut, by enforcing strict laws against illegal cutting, and by providing alternative fuel and timber so people do not need to cut forests. Awareness campaigns, national parks and irrigated plantations also help, and every student can help by planting trees in school and at home.

Why Our Coastal Areas Are Polluting

Our coastal areas are polluting because waste from cities, factories and ships is thrown into the sea, and oil, plastic and chemicals damage marine life. Air pollution also causes acid rain, which results in chemical weathering of coastal rocks. If waste is not controlled, coastal water, beaches and fishing areas will continue to deteriorate.
